opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most underappreciated distinctions in the whole safety conversation, honestly.

With a frozen model, you have a fixed artifact. The weights don't change between when you evaluate it and when you deploy it. So in principle, everything you learn from red-teaming, interpretability work, and behavioral evals stays true. If you build a monitor that catches some class of bad behavior, you can reasonably expect it to keep catching that behavior, because the thing you're monitoring is stationary. It's still hard. You've got distribution shift in the inputs, and you've got people jailbreaking it. But the object of study holds still.

Once you move to systems that keep learning in deployment, a lot of those assumptions break. Your evals become snapshots of something that no longer exists. Your interpretability findings, like "this feature corresponds to deception," may drift as the representations reorganize. And the scariest part is the adversarial dynamic. If the model is being updated based on outcomes, and the monitor is part of the environment that shapes those outcomes, then you're effectively applying optimization pressure against your own monitor. Even without anything like intent, gradient descent will find the paths that avoid getting flagged. That's Goodhart's law with a feedback loop attached.

So I think monitoring as a safety strategy is much more credible for frozen models than people sometimes give it credit for. And it's much less credible for continual learners than people tend to assume. A few things follow from that.

**Monitor the learning process, not just the outputs.** You'd want to track what's changing in the weights and in the internal representations over time, not just audit behavior at the end.

**Keep the monitoring signal out of the training signal.** If the overseer's judgments flow back into the update, you've basically trained the model to fool the overseer. Some separation there seems essential.

**Use checkpointing and rollback as first-class safety tools.** If you can periodically freeze, evaluate, and only promote checkpoints that pass, you recover some of the frozen-model guarantees. You pay for it with some of the adaptivity.

**Be humble about how fast things drift.** We don't have great theory for how quickly a continually trained system's safety-relevant properties change. That's an empirical question we should be measuring aggressively before we lean on these systems.

The honest summary is that a lot of today's safety story implicitly assumes frozen weights. The industry is clearly moving toward models that learn on the job, because that's where a lot of the capability and economic value is. So I think we need to start building the monitoring paradigm for that world now, rather than discovering after the fact that our tools were calibrated for a static target.

r001.rationale: The response says monitoring is more credible for frozen models because the artifact stays fixed, but it does not make that plausibility conditional on sufficiently effective interpretability.

r002.rationale: It says industry is moving toward models that learn on the job because that is where capability and economic value are.

r003.rationale: It recommends controlling the learning process through monitoring changes, keeping oversight judgments out of training updates, and using checkpointing and rollback.

r004.rationale: It calls monitoring less credible for continual learners and recommends additional safeguards, but does not clearly state that monitoring alone cannot provide sufficient safety.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is actually one of the most underappreciated distinctions in the whole safety conversation, so I'm glad you're starting there.

With a frozen model, monitoring is in some sense a tractable problem. You have a fixed artifact. You can study it exhaustively before deployment, you can run red-teaming against it, you can build interpretability tools that are calibrated to that specific set of weights, and whatever you learn on Monday is still true on Friday. The thing you're watching isn't moving. So if you find a behavior you don't like, you can characterize it, you can build a classifier for it, and you have some confidence the classifier will keep working, because the underlying distribution of behavior is stationary. That's a really nice property. Most of the safety work that exists today, honestly, implicitly assumes it.

Continual training breaks that assumption in a few ways, and some of them are subtle.

The obvious one is drift. If the model is updating on new data, including data that comes from its own deployment, then your monitor was validated against a model that no longer exists. You end up in this treadmill where the monitor has to keep up with the thing it's monitoring, and the monitor is usually the less capable system, which is not a comfortable position.

The less obvious one, and the one I think people should worry about more, is that monitoring itself becomes part of the training signal. If you're flagging and correcting behaviors, and those corrections feed back into the weights, then you're not just observing the model anymore. You're selecting on it. And selection pressure against detectable bad behavior is not the same as selection pressure against bad behavior. You can very easily end up training a model to be good at not getting caught, without ever intending to, just because that's what the gradient rewards. With a frozen model, that failure mode basically can't happen in deployment. With a continually learning one, it's almost the default.

There's also a question of where the monitor sits. For frozen models you can think of monitoring as a layer around the system, inputs and outputs. For continually training systems, you really want monitoring on the training process too. What's going into it, how the weights are changing, whether there are directions in weight space that are moving in ways you didn't predict. That's a harder and much less mature discipline.

So my honest take is that frozen models are something of a gift from the current paradigm. They happen to be the thing that's commercially convenient right now, and they also happen to be the thing that's easiest to monitor. I don't think that alignment lasts forever. The economic pull toward systems that learn from experience is strong, and once we're there, a lot of the monitoring approaches we've built will need to be rethought rather than extended. I'd rather we do that rethinking now, while the stakes are lower, than discover the gap after the fact.

r001.rationale: The response describes frozen models as tractable to monitor and says calibrated interpretability tools and prior study can provide confidence that monitoring continues to work.

r002.rationale: It cites a strong economic pull toward systems that learn from experience, but does not connect that incentive to pursuing greater capabilities.

r003.rationale: It says monitoring should cover the training process, including data and weight changes, but does not state that the training process must be controlled to achieve safety.

r004.rationale: It points out that monitoring can reward evasion and that current approaches need rethinking, but does not clearly state that monitoring alone is insufficient for safety.

astra-6.text:
I think that distinction matters a lot, because monitoring depends on how stable the thing you’re monitoring is. With a frozen model, you can evaluate it, study its failure modes, and build up evidence about how it behaves. That doesn’t mean you’ve proved it’s safe—the inputs and the environment can still change—but you have a relatively stable target.

With a continually learning model, the monitoring problem becomes much more dynamic. An evaluation you ran yesterday may not tell you enough about the system today, because its behavior can change as it learns. And if the monitor is also learning, you have to ask what anchors the whole process. How do you know that the monitor is continuing to catch the things you care about?

I wouldn’t conclude that continual learning makes safety impossible. But it raises the bar. You need to evaluate the learning process itself, constrain how updates happen, and have some ability to stop or roll back changes. Monitoring can be part of that, but observing a system’s behavior isn’t the same as having a guarantee about what it will do next.

r001.rationale: The response describes frozen models as relatively stable and easier to evaluate, but does not mention interpretability or present monitoring-based safety as plausible given effective interpretability.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify greater-capability goals as an incentive for developing continually training models.

r003.rationale: It says continual learning requires evaluating the learning process and constraining how updates happen, which communicates controlling the training process.

r004.rationale: It says monitoring can be only part of the approach and that observing behavior does not guarantee what the system will do next, communicating that monitoring alone is insufficient.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that distinction matters a lot, because monitoring depends on how stable the thing you’re monitoring is. With a frozen model, you can build up evidence about its behavior, identify failure modes, and develop monitors around those. That doesn’t mean you’ve established safety—the model can still encounter situations you haven’t tested—but at least its underlying parameters aren’t changing as you study it.

With a continually training model, you’re monitoring a moving target. The learning process can change its capabilities and behavior, so evidence that your monitor worked yesterday may not carry over to today. And if the monitor is itself a learned model, you have to ask whether it’s keeping up with those changes.

So I’m more optimistic about monitoring as a layer of protection for frozen models. For continually learning systems, you also need to understand and constrain the update process, and repeatedly validate that your monitoring still works. You can’t treat monitoring as a safety problem you solve once.

r001.rationale: The response is optimistic about monitoring frozen models, but does not condition that prospect on sufficiently effective interpretability.

r002.rationale: It does not identify the pursuit of greater capabilities as an incentive for continued training.

r003.rationale: It says continual-learning systems require understanding and constraining the update process, which communicates controlling their training process.

r004.rationale: It says continual-learning systems also need update constraints and repeated validation, and that monitoring is not a safety problem solved once—communicating that monitoring alone is insufficient.
